summary.text: Stratospheric aerosols are long-lived sulfate particles that form when sulfur dioxide from an eruption rises into the stratosphere and reacts with water vapor.
They reflect sunlight and cool the planet for a time, and after a large eruption they can stay aloft for a year or more.
Because this cooling happens naturally after eruptions, some have proposed deliberately injecting aerosols into the stratosphere to reduce global warming.

items.prompt: A volcano throws out a huge ash cloud along with sulfur dioxide gas. Which part ends up cooling the planet for a year or more?

options.label: The ash, which hangs in the air for decades
The sulfur gas, which forms high sulfate particles
The heat of the lava, which escapes to space
The steam, which falls back as snow worldwide

items.explain: Ash falls out fairly quickly, but sulfur dioxide rises into the stratosphere and forms long-lived sulfate particles that reflect sunlight.

items.prompt: After Mount Pinatubo erupted in 1991, roughly how much did global temperatures drop?

options.label: About 5 °C
About 0.05 °C
About 10 °C
About 0.5 °C

items.explain: The 1991 Pinatubo eruption cooled global temperatures by about 0.5 degrees Celsius for up to three years.

items.prompt: Why does a layer of sulfate particles high in the sky make the ground below cooler?

options.label: It bounces some sunlight back before it arrives
It traps heat close to the ground at night
It soaks up carbon dioxide from the air
It speeds up winds that carry heat away

items.explain: Sulfate aerosols reflect sunlight, which cools the planet; this raises albedo and dims incoming light.

items.prompt: One proposal to slow global warming takes its idea straight from what big eruptions do. What would it involve?

options.label: Pumping carbon dioxide into old volcanoes
Painting city roofs and roads white
Putting reflective particles high in the stratosphere
Planting forests on fresh lava fields

items.explain: Stratospheric aerosol injection would add aerosols to the stratosphere to create the dimming and higher albedo that volcanic winters cause naturally.

items.prompt: If people did try to spread aerosols in the stratosphere on purpose, what is the leading idea for getting them up there?

options.label: Setting off small volcanic eruptions
Firing them from cannons on mountaintops
Spraying them from ships at sea level
Flying them up in custom-built aircraft

items.explain: Custom aircraft are the leading proposed method of delivery.

items.prompt: Two eruptions release equal amounts of sulfur dioxide. In one the gas reaches the stratosphere; in the other it does not. Which cools the planet for longer?

options.label: The one whose gas reached the stratosphere
The one whose gas stayed lower down
Both cool for the same length of time
Neither, since sulfur gas warms the planet

items.explain: In the stratosphere the gas forms long-lived sulfate aerosols that reflect sunlight and can stay aloft for a year or more.

paragraphs.heading: Made by eruptions
paragraphs.text: Volcanic eruptions throw ash and gases into the air. The ash drops back out fairly quickly, but sulfur dioxide gas can rise into the stratosphere, high in the upper atmosphere. There it reacts with water vapor to make sulfate aerosols, particles that last a long time. After a big eruption, these particles can stay aloft for a year or more.

paragraphs.heading: A natural sunshade
paragraphs.text: The sulfate particles reflect sunlight and cool the planet for a while. Depending on its size, a large eruption can cool the globe for a short time by about half a degree or more. When Mount Pinatubo erupted in 1991, global temperatures dropped by about 0.5 °C for up to three years. Such events have played an important part in how Earth's climate has varied in the past.

paragraphs.heading: Other sources of aerosols
paragraphs.text: Volcanoes are not the only source. Oceans, deserts and living things make aerosols too: wind over waves throws up spray that is mostly sea salt, and plankton give off gases that end up as sulfate particles. People add more, mainly by burning fossil fuels and biomass, producing sulfates, nitrates, black carbon or soot, and organic carbon. Sulfates do most of the cooling, while black carbon absorbs light, warming the air and darkening snow and ice.

paragraphs.heading: Hiding some of the warming
paragraphs.text: Human-made aerosols have masked part of global warming. Between 1850 and 2014 they lowered average surface temperature by about 0.66 °C, more so in the more populous Northern Hemisphere, and that uneven cooling has changed rainfall, including weaker tropical monsoons. Since the 1980s, clean-air rules have cut sulfate pollution in Europe and North America, and more recently in China. The air is healthier, but losing that cooling has helped warming speed up.

paragraphs.heading: Copying the volcano
paragraphs.text: Some have proposed creating this effect on purpose to reduce global warming. Stratospheric aerosol injection would put aerosols into the stratosphere to dim sunlight and make Earth more reflective, as happens naturally in a volcanic winter. Mikhail Budyko is believed to have floated the idea of using sulfate aerosols this way in 1974, and such schemes are sometimes called a Budyko Blanket. The leading proposed way to deliver the particles is custom aircraft. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change calls it the most-researched method of its kind, and says there is high agreement it could hold warming under 1.5 °C, though it would do so imperfectly and other effects are possible.

paragraphs.heading: Open questions
paragraphs.text: Much is still unknown. Various forms of sulfur have cooled the planet after big eruptions, but as of 2021 research was thin, the aerosols already in the stratosphere were poorly understood, and no material was the clear favourite; alumina, calcite and salt are also being considered. In 2012 the UK's SPICE project planned a limited field test of a delivery system, but the test was cancelled. A separate field experiment called SCoPEx, described in 2015, still had no set time or place as of October 2020. When members of the public were consulted about the SPICE test, almost all were willing to let the trial go ahead, but very few were comfortable with actually using stratospheric aerosols.
